slides.title: The Second World War
slides.text: The recap: the Hitler–Stalin pact of August 1939 dividing east-central Europe into zones of interest, and the invasion of Poland bringing British and French declarations of war.

slides.title: Europe during the Cold War (1945–1955)
slides.text: Kamila Staudigl-Ciechowicz.

slides.title: Austria under Allied control
slides.text: THREE ANTI-FASCIST PARTIES proclaim Austria's independence and install a PROVISIONAL GOVERNMENT, with the goal of a QUICK RETURN TO DEMOCRATIC STRUCTURES — but the WESTERN ALLIES DO NOT WANT TO RECOGNISE IT UNTIL OCTOBER 1945. 4 JULY 1945: the FIRST ALLIED CONTROL AGREEMENT — concluded WITHOUT RENNER'S PARTICIPATION — giving the Allies supreme power, creating the ALLIED COUNCIL and four occupation zones. 25 NOVEMBER: the first elections — ÖVP 85 seats, SPÖ 76, KPÖ 4. 19 DECEMBER: the first session of the National Council, and the B-VG IS AGAIN IN FULL FORCE. 28 JUNE 1946: the SECOND ALLIED CONTROL AGREEMENT, under which ONLY CONSTITUTIONAL LAWS need Allied approval.

cards.q: Give the sequence of Austrian reconstruction in 1945/46 with dates.
cards.a: Three anti-fascist parties proclaim independence and form a provisional government, recognised by the Western Allies only in October 1945. 4 July 1945: First Allied Control Agreement — supreme Allied power, Allied Council, four zones. 25 November: first elections (ÖVP 85, SPÖ 76, KPÖ 4). 19 December: first sitting of the National Council, the B-VG again in full force. 28 June 1946: Second Allied Control Agreement.

cards.q: What was the result of the first Austrian elections of November 1945, and what does the KPÖ result show?
cards.a: ÖVP 85 seats, SPÖ 76, KPÖ 4. The communists won four seats despite Soviet occupation of part of the country — the Austrian communists had no popular base.

slides.title: Source: Article 6 of the Control Agreement
slides.text: ALL LEGISLATIVE MEASURES, as defined by the Allied Council, shall BEFORE THEY TAKE EFFECT OR ARE PUBLISHED be submitted by the Austrian Government to the Allied Council. IN THE CASE OF CONSTITUTIONAL LAWS, THE WRITTEN APPROVAL OF THE ALLIED COUNCIL IS REQUIRED. In the case of ALL OTHER legislative measures and international agreements, IT MAY BE ASSUMED THAT THE ALLIED COUNCIL HAS GIVEN ITS APPROVAL IF WITHIN THIRTY-ONE DAYS it has not objected. The technique is worth noting: constitutional law needs EXPRESS consent, ordinary law only needs SILENCE — a tacit-approval rule that hands most of the legislative process back while keeping the constitution under control.

cards.q: How did Article 6 of the Second Control Agreement treat constitutional law differently from ordinary law?
cards.a: Constitutional laws required the WRITTEN APPROVAL of the Allied Council before publication. For all other legislative measures and international agreements, approval was ASSUMED if the Council raised no objection within thirty-one days — express consent for the constitution, tacit consent for everything else.

slides.title: The two Control Agreements
slides.text: First Allied Control Agreement, 4 July 1945: the Allied Council created; recognition of the provisional state government in October 1945; approval of its laws by the Council necessary. Second Allied Control Agreement, 28 June 1946, after the first National Council elections: written approval required only for constitutional law.

slides.title: Austria and Germany compared
slides.text: SIMILARITIES: an Allied Control Council in both; division into FOUR OCCUPATION ZONES; and JOINT OCCUPATION OF THE CAPITAL — Berlin and Vienna. DIFFERENCES, and they decide everything that follows: some German territories are TRANSFERRED TO POLAND AND THE USSR with EXPULSION of the local population; there is NO GOVERNMENT FOR THE WHOLE OF GERMANY, so the ALLIED CONTROL COUNCIL LEGISLATES FOR GERMANY ITSELF; the Control Council BREAKS UP IN 1948; countries emerge within the individual zones; the western zones unite into a SINGLE ECONOMIC AREA in 1948; and in 1949 the FEDERAL REPUBLIC and the GERMAN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC are founded. Austria kept a government of its own for the whole country — which is why it stayed one state.

cards.q: What was the decisive difference between occupied Austria and occupied Germany?
cards.a: Austria had a government for the WHOLE country from 1945; Germany had none, so the Allied Control Council legislated for Germany itself. When the Council broke up in 1948, states formed inside the zones and in 1949 the Federal Republic and the GDR were founded — while Austria stayed one state.

cards.q: What did Austria and Germany have in common under occupation?
cards.a: An Allied Control Council, division into four occupation zones, and joint occupation of the capital — Berlin and Vienna.

slides.title: Berlin
slides.text: Jointly occupied by all four Allies from 1945, divided into four sectors — though SOVIET PATROLS CONTINUED THROUGHOUT BERLIN UNTIL 1990. From 1948 there is one mayor and one city parliament each for West and East Berlin. The GDR CLAIMS EAST BERLIN AS ITS CAPITAL. And the western side's own oddity: THE WESTERN ALLIES PREVENT WEST BERLIN FROM JOINING THE FEDERAL REPUBLIC — its representatives sit in the Bundestag only as ADVISORY MEMBERS WITHOUT VOTING RIGHTS. Both sides kept the four-power status they found convenient.

cards.q: Why was West Berlin not part of the Federal Republic?
cards.a: Because the WESTERN ALLIES prevented it, to preserve the four-power status of the city. West Berlin's representatives sat in the Bundestag only as advisory members without voting rights — while the GDR claimed East Berlin as its capital.

slides.title: Berlin in film
slides.text: Ulbricht on the building of the Wall, and Schabowski announcing its opening.

slides.title: The Wall
slides.text: The flow of refugees to the West leads to the CONSTRUCTION OF THE BERLIN WALL ON 13 AUGUST 1961. The WESTERN ALLIES DEPLOY TANKS and force the maintenance of their position throughout Berlin — insisting on the four-power right of movement in the whole city, which is why Soviet patrols also continued in the west until 1990.

cards.q: When was the Berlin Wall built, and how did the Western Allies respond?
cards.a: 13 August 1961, in response to the flow of refugees to the West. The Western Allies deployed tanks and forced the maintenance of their position throughout Berlin, insisting on the four-power right of movement in the whole city.

slides.title: The Prague Spring and the Brezhnev Doctrine
slides.text: The Czechoslovak Communist Party strives for reform — a SOCIALIST MARKET ECONOMY instead of a planned one. In 1968 the new First Secretary ALEXANDER DUBČEK wants COMMUNISM WITH A HUMANE FACE. On 21 AUGUST 1968 WARSAW PACT TROOPS — USSR, Poland, Hungary, Bulgaria — invade, and Dubček is imprisoned and deposed. The legal doctrine offered for it is the BREZHNEV DOCTRINE: ANY THREAT TO SOCIALIST RULE IN ANY STATE OF THE EASTERN BLOC IS A THREAT TO ALL OF THEM, AND THEREFORE JUSTIFIES THE INTERVENTION OF FELLOW SOCIALIST STATES. Note what it does to sovereignty: a state's internal political order becomes the alliance's business. ALBANIA protests, withdraws from the Warsaw Pact and falls into complete isolation.

terms.def: Any threat to socialist rule in one Eastern-bloc state is a threat to all, justifying intervention by fellow socialist states — limited sovereignty as a doctrine of international law.

cards.q: What is the Brezhnev Doctrine, and what does it do to sovereignty?
cards.a: That any threat to 'socialist rule' in any Eastern-bloc state is a threat to all of them and therefore justifies intervention by fellow socialist states. It makes a state's internal political order the alliance's business — sovereignty limited from within the bloc.

cards.q: What happened in Czechoslovakia in 1968, and which state protested?
cards.a: Dubček's reform course — 'communism with a humane face', a socialist market economy — was ended on 21 August 1968 when Warsaw Pact troops of the USSR, Poland, Hungary and Bulgaria invaded and deposed him. ALBANIA protested, withdrew from the Warsaw Pact and fell into complete isolation.

slides.title: Two economies, two organisations
slides.text: 1947: US Secretary of State GEORGE MARSHALL promises financial aid for Europe — the MARSHALL PLAN. 1948: the ORGANISATION FOR EUROPEAN ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION (OEEC) is founded. And the Austrian peculiarity: AUSTRIA IS ALLOWED TO PARTICIPATE IN THE OEEC ALTHOUGH PARTLY UNDER SOVIET OCCUPATION — UNLIKE CZECHOSLOVAKIA, which was not. 1949: the COUNCIL FOR MUTUAL ECONOMIC ASSISTANCE (COMECON) on the other side. Special status for FINLAND and YUGOSLAVIA; SPAIN isolated.

cards.q: How did Austria's position in the Marshall Plan differ from Czechoslovakia's?
cards.a: Austria was allowed to take part in the OEEC from 1948 despite being partly under Soviet occupation; Czechoslovakia was not. The economic division of Europe did not follow the occupation zones exactly.

slides.title: Where does European integration come from?
slides.text: The question put to the room before the answer.

slides.title: The Council of Europe and the ECHR
slides.text: Founded in 1949, with accessions through 1989 and a further wave after it — and in 2022 the EXPULSION OF RUSSIA. 1950: the EUROPEAN CONVENTION ON HUMAN RIGHTS. And the Austrian dates, which matter: Austria JOINS THE COUNCIL OF EUROPE IN 1956, ADOPTS THE ECHR IN 1958, and the Convention is RECOGNISED AS CONSTITUTIONAL LAW SINCE 1964. Remember the last one: the B-VG had no catalogue of fundamental rights, and the ECHR is how Austria finally acquired one at constitutional rank.

cards.q: Give the Austrian dates for the Council of Europe and the ECHR, and say why the last one matters.
cards.a: Austria joined the Council of Europe in 1956, adopted the ECHR in 1958, and the Convention has been recognised as CONSTITUTIONAL LAW since 1964. That matters because the B-VG was a 'torso' without a catalogue of fundamental rights — the ECHR is how Austria acquired one at constitutional rank.

slides.title: The Schuman Plan, 9 May 1950
slides.text: The French Government proposes that FRANCO-GERMAN PRODUCTION OF COAL AND STEEL AS A WHOLE BE PLACED UNDER A COMMON HIGH AUTHORITY, within an organization OPEN TO THE PARTICIPATION OF THE OTHER COUNTRIES OF EUROPE. Pooling coal and steel should provide common foundations for economic development AS A FIRST STEP IN THE FEDERATION OF EUROPE, and will change the destinies of regions long devoted to the manufacture of munitions of war, OF WHICH THEY HAVE BEEN THE MOST CONSTANT VICTIMS. And the sentence everything turns on: THE SOLIDARITY IN PRODUCTION THUS ESTABLISHED WILL MAKE IT PLAIN THAT ANY WAR BETWEEN FRANCE AND GERMANY BECOMES NOT MERELY UNTHINKABLE, BUT MATERIALLY IMPOSSIBLE. Not a declaration of friendship — a plan to remove the physical means of war by placing them under joint control.

cards.q: What does the Schuman Plan propose, and by what mechanism is it supposed to prevent war?
cards.a: That Franco-German coal and steel production as a whole be placed under a COMMON HIGH AUTHORITY, in an organisation open to other European countries, as a first step in the federation of Europe. The mechanism is material, not moral: pooling the means of making munitions makes war between France and Germany 'not merely unthinkable, but MATERIALLY IMPOSSIBLE'.

slides.title: The ECSC
slides.text: 1952: the Treaty on the European Coal and Steel Community, in force 1952–2002 — a common market for the production, trade and consumption of coal and steel.

slides.title: The ECSC's task
slides.text: To 'CONTRIBUTE TO ECONOMIC EXPANSION, THE DEVELOPMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND THE IMPROVEMENT OF THE STANDARD OF LIVING in the participating countries through the institution, in harmony with the general economy of the member States, of A COMMON MARKET'. The common market appears here as the INSTRUMENT, and prosperity and employment as the aim.

slides.title: The ECSC's organs — and today's EU
slides.text: Four organs, and each is the ancestor of a present one. HIGH AUTHORITY, today the COMMISSION: represents the interests OF THE COMMUNITY, INDEPENDENT OF THE MEMBER STATES — 'A SUPRANATIONAL CHARACTER'. COUNCIL OF MINISTERS, today the COUNCIL OF THE EU: the interests OF THE MEMBER STATES, staffed by ministers from national governments. COMMON ASSEMBLY, today the EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the interests OF THE PEOPLE — DIRECTLY ELECTED SINCE 1980. COURT OF JUSTICE: legal control, seat in LUXEMBOURG. The institutional triangle of community, states and people is there from 1952.

terms.def: The character of the High Authority — acting for the community and independent of the member states, as against an intergovernmental body composed of their representatives.

cards.q: Name the four ECSC organs, whose interests each represents, and their modern successors.
cards.a: High Authority — the community's interests, independent of the member states, 'supranational' — today the Commission. Council of Ministers — the member states' interests, ministers from national governments — today the Council of the EU. Common Assembly — the people's interests, directly elected since 1980 — today the European Parliament. Court of Justice — legal control, seat in Luxembourg.

slides.title: The problem behind European defence
slides.text: Hundreds of thousands of American soldiers have been stationed in Europe since 1945 — HOW TO WITHDRAW THEM? The US answer: WESTERN GERMANY MUST HAVE ITS OWN TROOPS AGAIN — which causes GREAT FEARS IN WESTERN EUROPE, especially FRANCE. Hence the idea of a COMMON WESTERN EUROPEAN ARMY IN WHICH NO COUNTRY MAY HAVE ITS OWN TROOPS ALONGSIDE IT. European integration in defence begins as a way of rearming Germany without giving Germany an army.

cards.q: What problem was the idea of a common European army meant to solve?
cards.a: How to withdraw the American troops stationed in Europe since 1945. The US insisted West Germany must have troops again, which alarmed western Europe and France above all — so a common European army was proposed in which no country would have its own troops alongside it: rearming Germany without giving Germany an army.

slides.title: The plan that failed
slides.text: The EUROPEAN POLITICAL COMMUNITY was projected for 1953 as the roof over two pillars: the ECSC and the EUROPEAN DEFENCE COMMUNITY. The EDC agreement was SIGNED IN 1953 AND NEVER REALISED; the European Political Community remained ONLY PROJECTED. European political union was attempted in 1953, failed, and integration then proceeded through the economy instead — which is why the EU is built out of a coal and steel community rather than a political one.

cards.q: What were the European Defence Community and the European Political Community, and what became of them?
cards.a: The EDC agreement was signed in 1953 and NEVER REALISED; the EPC, projected as a political roof over the ECSC and the EDC, remained only a project. Political union failed in 1953, so integration proceeded through the economy instead.

slides.title: The Paris Agreements, 23 October 1954 — and the symmetry
slides.text: SOVEREIGNTY FOR THE FEDERAL REPUBLIC, with small exceptions, and the END OF OCCUPATION; INTEGRATION OF THE BUNDESWEHR INTO NATO. And the EASTERN BLOC'S REACTION, point for point: SOVEREIGNTY FOR THE GDR with small exceptions and the end of occupation; the GDR gets its NATIONALE VOLKSARMEE; and on 14 MAY 1955 the WARSAW PACT is founded. Each step on one side is answered by the mirror step on the other — which is the structure of the Cold War in miniature.

cards.q: What did the Paris Agreements of 1954 bring, and how did the Eastern bloc answer?
cards.a: Sovereignty for the Federal Republic with small exceptions, the end of occupation, and the Bundeswehr integrated into NATO. The answer: sovereignty for the GDR and the end of occupation there, the Nationale Volksarmee, and the founding of the Warsaw Pact on 14 May 1955 — each step mirrored.

slides.title: Think – Pair – Share
slides.text: Three images from 1955, and the question of which event they refer to — with Figl's joke: 'and now, Raab, play the Reblaus, then they are ready to negotiate'.

slides.title: The State Treaty and neutrality, 1955
slides.text: Three dates, and the order of them is the whole point. 15 APRIL 1955: the MOSCOW MEMORANDUM — leading Austrian politicians PLEDGE NEUTRALITY AS THE PRICE FOR TROOP WITHDRAWAL, and it is NO FORMAL TREATY. 15 MAY: the STATE TREATY of Vienna-Belvedere, providing for the withdrawal of Allied troops by 25 October — AND NEUTRALITY IS NOT MENTIONED IN IT. 26 OCTOBER: the CONSTITUTIONAL LAW ON AUSTRIA'S PERMANENT NEUTRALITY, declared 'OF OUR OWN FREE WILL'. So neutrality was promised informally, deliberately left out of the treaty, and then enacted by Austria itself as a free decision — the legal form says free will, the sequence says price. PERMANENT NEUTRALITY on the Swiss model carries duties ALSO IN PEACETIME: the state must avoid anything that could draw it into a war — no military alliance, and arguably no customs union.

terms.def: Neutrality binding also in peacetime, on the Swiss model: the state must avoid anything that could draw it into a war — no military alliance, and arguably no customs union.

cards.q: Give the three steps of 1955 and explain why neutrality is not in the State Treaty.
cards.a: 15 April: the Moscow Memorandum, in which Austrian politicians pledge neutrality as the price of troop withdrawal — no formal treaty. 15 May: the State Treaty, providing for withdrawal by 25 October, WITHOUT mentioning neutrality. 26 October: the constitutional law on permanent neutrality, declared 'of our own free will'. Keeping it out of the treaty let Austria enact it as its own free decision rather than an imposed obligation.

cards.q: What duties does permanent neutrality impose, and when?
cards.a: Duties ALSO IN PEACETIME, on the Swiss model: the state must avoid anything that could draw it into a war — no military alliance, and arguably no customs union.

slides.title: The State Treaty
slides.text: The signing at the Belvedere, 15 May 1955.

slides.title: What the State Treaty contained
slides.text: PROHIBITION OF ANNEXATION TO GERMANY — the Anschlussverbot again, thirty-six years after Saint-Germain. DEMOCRACY, HUMAN RIGHTS, MINORITY RIGHTS. NO 'NAZI' ORGANISATIONS, AND NO HABSBURGS — the Habsburg Law of 1919 written into an international treaty. PROHIBITION OF ARMS, RESTITUTION, and MATERIAL OBLIGATIONS TOWARDS THE USSR.

cards.q: Name the contents of the Austrian State Treaty of 1955.
cards.a: Prohibition of annexation to Germany; democracy, human rights and minority rights; no 'Nazi' organisations and no Habsburgs; prohibition of certain arms; restitution; and material obligations towards the USSR.

cards.q: Which two older Austrian legal decisions reappear in the State Treaty of 1955?
cards.a: The prohibition of union with Germany, first imposed by Article 88 of Saint-Germain in 1919; and the exclusion of the Habsburgs, from the Habsburg Law of 1919 — both now written into an international treaty.
